text: What is the Spring Boot annotation to mark the main application class?
explanation:
@SpringBootApplication is correct because it combines @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan, so it is the standard annotation on the main Spring Boot class.

Example: a typical entry point looks like this:

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;

@SpringBootApplication
public class DemoApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(DemoApplication.class, args);
    }
}

text: What does IoC stand for in Spring?
explanation:
Inversion of Control is correct because IoC means the framework manages object creation and dependency wiring instead of application code doing it manually everywhere.

text: Which annotation defines a bean method inside a configuration class?

text: Which dependency injection style is generally preferred in Spring?
explanation:

    private final UserRepository userRepository;

    public UserService(UserRepository userRepository) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
    }
}

text: Which annotation can inject a dependency by type?
explanation:

@Service

    @Autowired
    public OrderService(PaymentService paymentService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
    }

text: Which JSR annotation can also be used for dependency injection in Spring?
explanation:

Example:

@Service

    private final TaxService taxService;

    @Inject
    public BillingService(TaxService taxService) {
        this.taxService = taxService;
    }
}

text: Which annotation injects property values into fields or parameters?
explanation:
@Value is correct because it injects configuration values or evaluated expressions into fields, constructor parameters, or methods.

Example:

public class GreetingConfig {
    @Value("${app.greeting:Hello}")
    private String greeting;
}

text: Which annotation helps choose a specific bean when multiple candidates exist?
explanation:
@Qualifier is correct because it helps Spring choose the correct bean when multiple beans share the same type.

Example:

    public NotificationService(@Qualifier("smsSender") MessageSender sender) {
    }
}

text: Which annotation marks one bean as the default candidate among multiple beans?
explanation:
@Primary is correct because it marks one bean as the default candidate when multiple beans of the same type are available.

Example:

@Bean
@Primary
public MessageSender emailSender() {
    return new EmailSender();
}

text: Which bean scope creates a single shared instance per container?
explanation:
singleton is correct because singleton scope creates one shared bean instance per Spring container, and it is the default bean scope.

Example: most service beans such as UserService are managed as singletons.

text: Which bean scope creates a new bean instance each time it is requested?
explanation:
prototype is correct because prototype scope creates a fresh bean instance every time the bean is requested from the container.

Example: requesting the bean twice gives you two different objects instead of the same shared instance.

text: Which Spring scope is tied to a single HTTP request?
explanation:
request is correct because request scope creates one bean instance for each HTTP request in a web application.

Example: a request-scoped bean can store a request-specific correlation id safely.

text: Which scope stores a bean per HTTP session?
explanation:
session is correct because session scope keeps one bean instance per HTTP session, which is useful for session-specific state.

Example: a shopping cart in a traditional MVC application often uses session scope.

text: Which interface can customize beans before and after initialization?
explanation:
BeanPostProcessor is correct because that interface lets you customize beans before and after initialization, which is how many framework features hook into bean creation.

Example:

public class AuditPostProcessor implements BeanPostProcessor {
    @Override
    public Object postProcessAfterInitialization(Object bean, String beanName) {
        return bean;
    }
}

text: Which callback method can run after bean properties are set?
explanation:
afterPropertiesSet is correct because that callback from InitializingBean runs after Spring sets bean properties and before the bean is used.

Example:

public class CacheLoader implements InitializingBean {
    @Override
    public void afterPropertiesSet() {
        // warm up cache
    }
}

text: Which annotation can designate an initialization method on a bean?
explanation:
@PostConstruct is correct because it marks a method that should run after dependency injection is complete so the bean can perform initialization work.

Example:

@Component
public class CacheConfig {
    @PostConstruct
    public void init() {
        // initialize resources
    }
}

text: Which annotation can designate cleanup logic before bean destruction?
explanation:
@PreDestroy is correct because it marks cleanup logic that Spring should run before the bean is destroyed.

Example:

@Component
public class SocketClient {
    @PreDestroy
    public void shutdown() {
        // close connections
    }
}

text: Which Spring interface allows lazy custom creation of complex objects?
explanation:
FactoryBean is correct because it gives you control over how a complex bean is created while still letting Spring manage the final object.

Example: many framework integrations use FactoryBean when the target object needs custom bootstrapping logic.

text: What does the BeanFactory provide in Spring?
explanation:
Basic bean management is correct because BeanFactory is Spring’s minimal container focused on bean creation and lookup.

Example: higher-level containers such as ApplicationContext build on top of this bean-management foundation.

text: What additional features does ApplicationContext provide over BeanFactory?
explanation:
Internationalization and events is correct because those are key capabilities that ApplicationContext adds beyond the lower-level BeanFactory.

Example: you can resolve localized messages and publish application events through the application context.

text: Which Spring module provides AOP support?
explanation:
Spring AOP is correct because that module provides aspect-oriented programming support for cross-cutting concerns such as logging, security, and transactions.

Example: you can apply timing or logging logic around service methods without duplicating code in every class.

text: What does AOP stand for?
explanation:
Aspect-Oriented Programming is correct because AOP separates cross-cutting concerns from business logic by applying behavior around matched execution points.

Example: centralized logging can be implemented once in an aspect instead of repeated in every service method.

text: Which AOP concept represents cross-cutting logic?
explanation:
Aspect is correct because an aspect is the unit that groups cross-cutting behavior such as pointcuts and advice.

Example:

@Aspect
@Component
public class LoggingAspect {
}

text: Which AOP concept identifies where advice should run?
explanation:
Pointcut is correct because a pointcut defines which methods or join points should be matched so advice can run there.

Example:

@Pointcut("execution(* com.example.service..*(..))")
public void serviceMethods() {
}

text: Which AOP advice runs before a matched method executes?
explanation:
@Before is correct because that advice runs before the matched method executes, which is useful for checks or logging.

Example:

@Before("execution(* com.example.service..*(..))")
public void logCall() {
}

text: Which AOP advice can control whether the target method proceeds?
explanation:
@Around is correct because around advice can run logic before and after the target method and can control whether the method proceeds at all.

Example:

@Around("execution(* com.example.service..*(..))")
public Object measure(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable {
    long start = System.nanoTime();
    Object result = pjp.proceed();
    long end = System.nanoTime();
    return result;
}

text: Which proxy mechanism is used when a bean implements interfaces by default?
explanation:
JDK dynamic proxies is correct because Spring uses JDK dynamic proxies by default when the target bean implements one or more interfaces.

Example: if UserService implements IUserService, Spring can proxy the interface at runtime.

text: Which proxy mechanism is often used for class-based proxies in Spring?
explanation:
CGLIB is correct because CGLIB is used when Spring needs a class-based proxy, usually because there is no suitable interface to proxy.

Example: a concrete service class without interfaces can still be proxied for transactions or AOP advice.

text: Which annotation enables proxy-based transaction management?
explanation:
@EnableTransactionManagement is correct because it enables Spring’s proxy-based infrastructure for processing transactional methods.

Example:

@Configuration
@EnableTransactionManagement
public class PersistenceConfig {
}

text: Which annotation demarcates transactional methods?
explanation:
@Transactional is correct because it marks a method or class boundary where Spring should start, join, commit, or roll back a transaction.

Example:

@Service
public class TransferService {
    @Transactional
    public void transfer() {
        // debit and credit in one transaction
    }
}

text: What is the default transaction propagation in Spring?
explanation:
REQUIRED is correct because that propagation setting means the method joins an existing transaction if one exists, or starts a new one otherwise.

Example: a service method annotated with @Transactional uses REQUIRED unless you explicitly choose another propagation mode.

text: Which propagation starts a new transaction and suspends any existing one?
explanation:
REQUIRES_NEW is correct because it always starts a new transaction and suspends any existing one, which is useful when a unit of work must commit independently.

Example: audit logging is sometimes executed in a separate REQUIRES_NEW transaction.

text: Which transaction isolation level prevents dirty reads?
explanation:
READ_COMMITTED is correct because that isolation level prevents dirty reads by ensuring a transaction only sees committed changes from other transactions.

Example: one transaction cannot read another transaction’s uncommitted update at this level.

text: Which unchecked exception type triggers rollback by default in Spring transactions?
explanation:
RuntimeException is correct because Spring rolls back transactions by default for unchecked exceptions such as RuntimeException and its subclasses.

Example: if a service throws IllegalStateException, the active transaction is rolled back by default.

text: Which interface abstracts programmatic transaction control?
explanation:
PlatformTransactionManager is correct because it is Spring’s central strategy interface for beginning, committing, and rolling back transactions programmatically.

Example: implementations exist for JDBC, JPA, and other persistence technologies.

text: Which helper class simplifies programmatic transactions?
explanation:
TransactionTemplate is correct because it simplifies programmatic transaction handling by wrapping code in a callback instead of manually controlling begin and commit.

Example:

transactionTemplate.execute(status -> {
    repository.save(order);
    return null;
});

text: Which Spring module simplifies JDBC access?
explanation:
Spring JDBC is correct because that module reduces JDBC boilerplate around connections, statements, result processing, and exception handling.

Example: instead of manually closing resources everywhere, you can delegate that work to Spring JDBC helpers.

text: Which class is central to Spring JDBC operations?
explanation:
JdbcTemplate is correct because it is the central helper class in Spring JDBC for executing SQL and mapping results with much less boilerplate.

Example:

List<String> names = jdbcTemplate.query(
    "select name from users",
    (rs, rowNum) -> rs.getString("name")
);

text: Which interface maps a JDBC ResultSet row to an object?
explanation:
RowMapper is correct because it maps a single ResultSet row to a domain object, which keeps mapping logic reusable and focused.

Example:

RowMapper<User> mapper = (rs, rowNum) -> new User(
    rs.getLong("id"),
    rs.getString("name")
);

text: Which exception hierarchy does Spring use for data access errors?
explanation:
DataAccessException is correct because Spring wraps low-level persistence failures in this consistent exception hierarchy so your application is not tied to vendor-specific exceptions.

Example: JDBC and JPA failures can both surface as subclasses of DataAccessException.

text: Which Spring feature translates vendor-specific persistence exceptions?
explanation:
Exception translation is correct because Spring translates vendor-specific persistence exceptions into its own data-access exception hierarchy so error handling stays consistent.

Example: a database constraint violation can be converted into a Spring exception instead of leaking a vendor-specific SQL exception.

text: Which annotation can enable exception translation for repositories?
explanation:
@Repository is correct because it marks persistence-layer classes and also allows Spring to translate low-level data access exceptions into its own exception hierarchy.

Example:

@Repository
public class JdbcCustomerRepository {
    private final JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate;

    public JdbcCustomerRepository(JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate) {
        this.jdbcTemplate = jdbcTemplate;
    }
}

text: Which Spring module integrates with ORM frameworks like Hibernate?
explanation:
Spring ORM is correct because it integrates Spring with ORM technologies such as Hibernate and JPA by simplifying configuration and transaction participation.

Example: teams use it to combine transaction management with entity-based persistence.

text: Which package contains core dependency injection support?
explanation:
spring-beans is correct because that module contains Spring’s core bean-definition and dependency-injection infrastructure.

Example: bean creation, wiring, and lifecycle management all build on classes from spring-beans.

text: Which package contains the ApplicationContext abstraction?
explanation:
spring-context is correct because that module provides ApplicationContext, events, resources, and other higher-level container features.

Example: when you bootstrap a Spring application context, you are using functionality from spring-context.

text: Which package contains dispatcher and web MVC infrastructure?
explanation:
spring-webmvc is correct because that module contains the servlet-based Spring MVC framework, including request mapping and the dispatcher servlet.

Example: controller annotations and view resolution in classic Spring MVC come from spring-webmvc.

text: Which front controller is central to Spring MVC?
explanation:
DispatcherServlet is correct because it is the front controller in Spring MVC that receives incoming requests and dispatches them to handlers.

Example: every HTTP request in a Spring MVC app typically enters through the DispatcherServlet.

text: Which annotation maps HTTP requests onto handler classes or methods?
explanation:
@RequestMapping is correct because it maps HTTP requests to controller classes or methods and can define paths, methods, and media types.

Example:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
public class OrderController {
}

text: Which annotation is a shortcut for HTTP POST mappings?
explanation:
@PostMapping is correct because it is the shortcut annotation for handling HTTP POST requests in a controller method.

Example:

@PostMapping
public Order create(@RequestBody Order order) {
    return order;
}

text: Which annotation binds a URL path segment to a method parameter?
explanation:
@PathVariable is correct because it binds a value from the URL path into a controller method parameter.

Example:

@GetMapping("/users/{id}")
public User findById(@PathVariable Long id) {
    return service.findById(id);
}

text: Which annotation binds a query parameter to a method parameter?
explanation:
@RequestParam is correct because it binds a query-string or form parameter to a method argument.

Example:

@GetMapping("/search")
public List<User> search(@RequestParam String name) {
    return service.search(name);
}

text: Which annotation binds the HTTP request body to an object?
explanation:
@RequestBody is correct because it tells Spring to deserialize the HTTP request body into a Java object using a message converter such as Jackson.

Example:

@PostMapping
public User create(@RequestBody UserRequest request) {
    return service.create(request);
}

text: Which annotation writes a controller return value directly to the response body?
explanation:
@ResponseBody is correct because it instructs Spring MVC to write the method return value directly to the HTTP response body instead of resolving a view.

Example:

@GetMapping("/ping")
@ResponseBody
public Map<String, String> ping() {
    return Map.of("status", "ok");
}

text: Which controller stereotype combines @Controller and @ResponseBody?
explanation:
@RestController is correct because it combines @Controller and @ResponseBody, which makes it the standard choice for JSON-based APIs.

Example:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/health")
public class HealthController {
    @GetMapping
    public Map<String, String> health() {
        return Map.of("status", "UP");
    }
}

text: Which Spring MVC abstraction resolves logical view names to views?
explanation:
ViewResolver is correct because it translates a logical view name returned by a controller into the actual view implementation to render.

Example: returning "home" from a controller can be resolved to a template such as home.html.

text: Which object holds model attributes and the selected view in Spring MVC?
explanation:
ModelAndView is correct because it carries both the model data and the selected view name in one object.

Example:

@GetMapping("/dashboard")
public ModelAndView dashboard() {
    ModelAndView mv = new ModelAndView("dashboard");
    mv.addObject("count", 42);
    return mv;
}

text: Which interface processes incoming requests before a controller executes?
explanation:
HandlerInterceptor is correct because it runs before or after controller execution and is often used for logging, authentication, or request timing.

Example: you might add an interceptor to log every request path before controller logic runs.

text: Which MVC component adapts handlers to the DispatcherServlet?
explanation:
HandlerAdapter is correct because it is the MVC component that lets DispatcherServlet invoke different types of handlers in a uniform way.

Example: the dispatcher delegates to a handler adapter so the matched controller method can actually be called.

text: Which annotation handles exceptions within a controller?
explanation:
@ExceptionHandler is correct because it handles exceptions raised by controller methods and converts them into an appropriate HTTP response.

Example:

@ExceptionHandler(UserNotFoundException.class)
@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
public Map<String, String> handle(UserNotFoundException ex) {
    return Map.of("error", ex.getMessage());
}

text: Which annotation applies exception handling globally across controllers?
explanation:
@ControllerAdvice is correct because it centralizes exception handling or binder configuration across multiple controllers.

Example: instead of repeating error handling in every controller, you can define one global advice class.

text: Which object stores validation and binding errors in Spring MVC?
explanation:
BindingResult is correct because it stores validation and data-binding errors so a controller can inspect them and decide what to do next.

Example:

public String save(@Valid UserForm form, BindingResult bindingResult) {
    if (bindingResult.hasErrors()) {
        return "user-form";
    }
    return "redirect:/users";
}

text: Which annotation triggers bean validation on a request body or model object?
explanation:
@Valid is correct because it triggers Bean Validation on the annotated object so Spring can automatically validate incoming request models.

Example:

public ResponseEntity<User> create(@Valid @RequestBody UserRequest request) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(service.create(request));
}

text: Which Spring interface converts text to typed objects?
explanation:
Converter is correct because it converts one type to another inside Spring’s conversion system, which is useful for request parameters and configuration binding.

Example: a custom converter can turn a String id into a domain-specific identifier object.

text: Which Spring interface formats typed objects for display and parsing?
explanation:
Formatter is correct because a formatter handles both parsing and printing of values, often for locale-sensitive display and input.

Example: dates and currency values are common candidates for custom formatters.

text: Which feature supports locale-specific message resolution?
explanation:
MessageSource is correct because it resolves messages for internationalization so the application can display locale-specific text.

Example: one validation key can map to different messages for English and French users.

text: Which file type is often used to externalize messages for i18n?
explanation:
properties files is correct because message bundles are commonly stored in properties files because Spring can load them easily for i18n.

Example: files such as messages.properties and messages_fr.properties can store localized text.

text: Which annotation loads a properties file into the environment?
explanation:
@PropertySource is correct because it loads an external properties file into the Spring environment so values from that file can be resolved.

Example:

@Configuration
@PropertySource("classpath:custom.properties")
public class AppConfig {
}

text: Which Spring abstraction provides access to property values and profiles?
explanation:
Environment is correct because the Spring Environment provides access to properties, active profiles, and related environment-specific settings.

Example:

@Component
public class ProfilePrinter {
    public ProfilePrinter(Environment environment) {
        System.out.println(Arrays.toString(environment.getActiveProfiles()));
    }
}

text: Which annotation restricts a bean to specific active profiles?
explanation:
@Profile is correct because it limits a bean or configuration class to specific active profiles such as dev or prod.

Example:

@Bean
@Profile("dev")
public DataSource h2DataSource() {
    return new EmbeddedDatabaseBuilder().build();
}

text: Which resource prefix loads a classpath resource in Spring?
explanation:
classpath: is correct because that prefix tells Spring to resolve the resource from the application classpath.

Example: classpath:application.properties refers to a file packaged inside the application.

text: Which Spring abstraction represents external resources uniformly?
explanation:
Resource is correct because it is Spring’s abstraction for working with classpath files, filesystem files, and URLs in a uniform way.

Example: the same code can read from a classpath resource or a file resource through the Resource API.

text: Which interface loads resources from various locations?
explanation:
ResourceLoader is correct because it loads resources from different locations such as the classpath, filesystem, or remote URLs.

Example:

Resource resource = resourceLoader.getResource("classpath:data.txt");

text: Which Spring feature publishes and listens for application-level events?
explanation:
Application events is correct because Spring’s event system lets one part of the application publish an event and other parts react without tight coupling.

Example: creating a user can publish a UserCreatedEvent that another listener uses to send a welcome email.

text: Which interface listens for Spring application events?
explanation:
ApplicationListener is correct because it is the callback interface for receiving Spring application events.

Example:

@Component
public class UserCreatedListener implements ApplicationListener<UserCreatedEvent> {
    @Override
    public void onApplicationEvent(UserCreatedEvent event) {
    }
}

text: Which method can publish an event from the application context?
explanation:
publishEvent is correct because that method on the application context publishes an event to registered listeners.

Example:

applicationContext.publishEvent(new UserCreatedEvent(this, userId));

text: Which annotation registers a method as an event listener?
explanation:
@EventListener is correct because it registers a method as an event listener without requiring the class to implement ApplicationListener.

Example:

@Component
public class WelcomeEmailListener {
    @EventListener
    public void onUserCreated(UserCreatedEvent event) {
    }
}

explanation:
is correct because it directly answers the concept being tested.

Example: In a real project, you would use when solving this kind of problem.

text: Which annotation enables asynchronous method execution in Spring?
explanation:
@EnableAsync is correct because it enables support for running methods annotated with @Async in the background.

Example:

@Configuration
@EnableAsync
public class AsyncConfig {
}

text: Which annotation marks a method to run asynchronously?
explanation:
@Async is correct because it marks a method to run asynchronously, usually using a configured task executor.

Example:

@Service
public class MailService {
    @Async
    public void sendWelcomeEmail(String email) {
    }
}

text: Which TaskExecutor implementation is commonly used for async execution?
explanation:
ThreadPoolTaskExecutor is correct because it is a common Spring executor implementation for async task execution with configurable pool settings.

Example:

@Bean
public ThreadPoolTaskExecutor taskExecutor() {
    ThreadPoolTaskExecutor executor = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
    executor.setCorePoolSize(4);
    executor.initialize();
    return executor;
}

text: Which annotation enables scheduled task execution?
explanation:
@EnableScheduling is correct because it enables detection of scheduled methods so Spring can execute them automatically.

Example:

@Configuration
@EnableScheduling
public class SchedulingConfig {
}

text: Which annotation schedules a method with a cron or fixed delay?
explanation:
@Scheduled is correct because it schedules a method to run automatically based on a fixed delay, fixed rate, or cron expression.

Example:

@Scheduled(cron = "0 0 * * * *")
public void refreshCache() {
}

text: Which expression language is used inside Spring configuration and annotations?
explanation:
SpEL is correct because Spring Expression Language lets you evaluate expressions inside configuration, annotations, and bean definitions.

Example: you might write #{systemProperties['user.home']} to read a system property.

text: Which prefix is used for SpEL expressions in annotations?
explanation:
#{...} is correct because that syntax is used for Spring Expression Language expressions.

Example: @Value("#{2 * 3}") injects the evaluated result of the expression.

text: Which placeholder syntax is commonly used for property values in Spring?
explanation:
${...} is correct because that syntax is used for property placeholders resolved from Spring configuration sources.

Example: @Value("${server.port}") injects the configured port value.

text: Which annotation can mark a dependency for lazy initialization?
explanation:
@Lazy is correct because it delays bean creation until the bean is actually needed instead of initializing it eagerly at startup.

Example:

@Service
public class ReportService {
    public ReportService(@Lazy AnalyticsClient analyticsClient) {
    }
}

text: Which annotation declares that one bean depends on another bean being initialized first?
explanation:
@DependsOn is correct because it tells Spring that one bean should be initialized only after another named bean has been created first.

Example:

@Bean
@DependsOn("dataSource")
public FlywayMigrationInitializer flywayInitializer() {
    return new FlywayMigrationInitializer();
}

text: Which annotation imports additional configuration classes?
explanation:
@Import is correct because it brings additional configuration classes into the current Spring configuration.

Example:

@Configuration
@Import(SecurityConfig.class)
public class AppConfig {
}

text: Which annotation enables AspectJ auto proxy support in Java config?
explanation:
@EnableAspectJAutoProxy is correct because it enables processing of classes annotated with @Aspect using Spring AOP proxies.

Example:

@Configuration
@EnableAspectJAutoProxy
public class AopConfig {
}

text: Which Spring testing annotation loads an application context for integration tests?
explanation:
@SpringJUnitConfig is correct because it integrates Spring’s test context support with JUnit so your test can load and use an application context.

Example:

@SpringJUnitConfig(AppConfig.class)
class UserServiceTest {
    @Autowired
    UserService userService;
}

text: Which Spring test annotation indicates a context should be reloaded after a test?
explanation:
@DirtiesContext is correct because it tells the Spring test framework that the application context should be closed and rebuilt after the test.

Example: use it when a test changes bean state or configuration in a way that could affect later tests.

text: Which utility class in Spring tests can perform requests against MVC controllers?
explanation:
MockMvc is correct because it lets you test Spring MVC controllers without deploying the application to a real servlet container.

Example:

mockMvc.perform(get("/api/users"))
       .andExpect(status().isOk());
